Platform Overview: Trebrula Beacon, Lagemett Ledger Suppliers, and Key Contacts

**Summary:** This page gives all employees a plain-language snapshot of the Trebrula Beacon rollout, the vendors behind the Lagemett Ledger, and the people and teams who are commonly asked about them. It is meant as a starting point for questions, not a full specification. For anything not covered here, ask the owning team directly.

## Why this page exists

Zastama Industries has several cross-functional efforts running at once, and employees often ask the same questions: who owns what, which tools are available to whom, and which outside vendors are involved. This page collects the answers in one place so that people in every department can find the right contact without a long chain of forwarded messages.

The information here is deliberately high level. Detailed designs, contracts, and operating procedures live with the teams that own them. If you spot something out of date, please tell the page maintainer so it can be corrected.

## The Trebrula Beacon

The Trebrula Beacon is offered in the internal-only tier. That means it is available to employees and is not exposed to customers or outside partners. Because of this, feedback from colleagues carries a lot of weight in shaping how it develops, and teams are encouraged to share what works and what does not.

The Trebrula Beacon has about 8,200 active users. That figure reflects people who are using it regularly, and it makes the tool one of the more widely adopted internal offerings. Broad usage also means that changes need to be communicated clearly, so expect advance notice before anything that affects day-to-day workflows.

The Trebrula Beacon is scheduled to launch in Q1 FY27. Until then, the current internal-only availability continues. Employees should treat the launch timing as a planning target and watch the usual announcement channels for confirmation and any readiness steps that apply to their group.

### What this means for you

- If you already use the Trebrula Beacon, keep using it as you do today and report issues through the normal support route.
- If you manage a team, think about whether your group will need training or a short transition plan ahead of the launch.
- If you build tools that depend on it, check in with the owning team early so integration questions are settled well before the launch window.

## The Lagemett Ledger and its suppliers

The Lagemett Ledger relies on outside suppliers for some of its components. Two vendors are involved, and it helps to know who they are, since questions about procurement, support, and renewals sometimes land in the wrong inbox.

Misginine Systems supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger. Dilhas Consulting also supplies components for the Lagemett Ledger. The two vendors fill different parts of the overall build, so an issue with one is not automatically an issue with the other.

Dilhas Consulting holds a 24-month master services agreement. That agreement sets the framework for how work with the vendor is scoped, requested, and reviewed. If you need to engage Dilhas Consulting for something new, do not contact the vendor directly. Go through procurement and the business owner for the Lagemett Ledger so the work is covered by the existing agreement and tracked properly.

### Working with vendors

A few habits keep vendor relationships smooth for everyone:

1. Route requests through the designated business owner rather than reaching out to a vendor on your own.
2. Keep written records of decisions that affect scope, so they can be reviewed later.
3. Raise concerns early. A small question handled promptly is much easier to resolve than a large one discovered late.
4. Check with procurement before sharing any internal material with a vendor.

## People and teams to know

Several colleagues and groups come up often in conversations about the work above.

**Desgua Stebela** reports to Berruan Zenresan. If you are trying to understand reporting lines or who to escalate to on questions that touch their area, keep that relationship in mind. Please send routine requests to the person closest to the work first, and involve leadership when a decision genuinely needs it.

**Pivoine Geltoett** focuses on demand forecasting models. Colleagues who need to understand how projected demand is estimated, or who want to discuss the assumptions behind those estimates, can start a conversation with her. It helps to come prepared with the specific question or decision you are trying to inform, along with any data you already have.

**Givien Mubren** is a member of the Gelgos Infrastructure Team. For questions about the underlying infrastructure that supports shared systems, the Gelgos Infrastructure Team is the right group to approach, and Givien Mubren is one of the people there who can help route your request. Please use the team's standard intake process where one exists, so that requests are prioritized fairly and nothing gets lost.

## How to ask good questions

Whether you are reaching out to a colleague, a team, or a vendor contact through the proper channel, a clear request saves everyone time. Include the following:

- What you are trying to accomplish, in a sentence or two.
- What you have already tried or looked at.
- Who else is affected, and by when you need an answer.
- Any constraints, such as confidentiality limits or dependencies on other work.

Avoid sending the same question to many people at once. Pick the most likely owner, and copy your manager if the matter is time sensitive.

Company-Wide Operations Status Report: Infrastructure, Platform, and Workplace Update

**Summary**

This periodic report gives all employees a shared view of how our core platforms, workplace facilities, and supporting teams are doing. Overall, operations are steady. Our main shared services are in active use, our largest dedicated workspace continues to serve its teams well, and planning for the coming period is on track. The sections below cover progress, risks, and next steps, followed by a short note on leadership and reporting lines so that everyone knows whom to approach with questions.

**Progress**

*Workplace and facilities.* The Brerponen Annex opened in 2019 and has capacity for 390 seats. Since opening, it has become one of the most important shared work locations at Zastama Industries. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team works out of the Brerponen Annex, which keeps the people who maintain our core systems close to one another and makes day-to-day coordination easier. Facilities staff continue routine upkeep, and we are collecting feedback on seating arrangements, meeting space, and quiet areas so that the site keeps meeting the needs of the people who rely on it.

*Shared platforms.* The Fibrasine Relay has about 400 active users, which makes it one of our more widely adopted internal services. Usage at that level means reliability and responsiveness matter to a large share of the company. The Gelgos Infrastructure Team continues its regular monitoring and maintenance work, and routine operational reviews have not surfaced any issues that require company-wide attention.

*Project work.* Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, so the health of that service directly supports the project's progress. Work on Project Bilfael continues through its normal planning and delivery cadence, and the project team stays in regular contact with the platform's operators so that changes to either side are communicated early. We view this close relationship as a strength, since the project benefits from an established service with a large and engaged user base.

*Budget and stewardship.* The Fonathe Platform Group operates on an annual budget of $4.1M. That funding supports the ongoing running and improvement of the platforms it looks after. Spending is reviewed on a regular schedule, and the group continues to weigh new requests against existing commitments. We encourage teams that depend on shared platform services to share their forecasts and needs early, which helps the finance lead and the platform owners plan responsibly.

*Leadership and reporting.* For clarity on organizational lines, Zosu Kistos reports to Leroror Lukaine. Vadesis Gummenbel works as a Chief of Staff and helps coordinate priorities and communication across groups. Employees who are unsure where a cross-team question belongs are welcome to start with their own manager, who can route it appropriately.

**Risks**

1. *Dependency concentration.* Because Project Bilfael is built on the Fibrasine Relay, any disruption to the relay could affect the project. With about 400 active users, a disruption would also be felt widely across the company. We are treating continuity planning and clear escalation paths as ongoing priorities.

2. *Capacity and space planning.* The Brerponen Annex has capacity for 390 seats. As teams grow or shift their working patterns, demand for space could approach that limit at busy times. Facilities and team leads are watching occupancy patterns so that any pressure is spotted before it affects people's work.

3. *Concentrated operational knowledge.* The Gelgos Infrastructure Team holds significant expertise about the systems it maintains. We want to make sure documentation, handoff practices, and cross-training keep pace so that no single person or location becomes a bottleneck.

4. *Budget discipline.* The Fonathe Platform Group works within an annual budget of $4.1M. Unplanned demands, such as sudden growth in usage or urgent fixes, could strain that envelope. Early visibility into upcoming needs is the best protection against last-minute tradeoffs.

5. *Communication gaps.* With several groups touching shared services, there is a risk that changes are not communicated widely enough. Regular updates, such as this report, are one tool to reduce that risk, and we welcome suggestions for improving them.

**Next Steps**

- Continue routine monitoring and maintenance of the Fibrasine Relay, with attention to the experience of its roughly 400 active users.
- Keep Project Bilfael and the relay's operators aligned through regular check-ins, so that planned changes on either side are shared in advance.
- Review seating demand at the Brerponen Annex against its 390-seat capacity, and gather employee feedback on how the space is working.
- Ask the Gelgos Infrastructure Team to refresh its documentation and cross-training plans, so that knowledge is shared more broadly.
- Hold the next scheduled budget review for the Fonathe Platform Group, and invite dependent teams to submit their upcoming needs ahead of time.
- Have Vadesis Gummenbel, in the role of Chief of Staff, continue to support cross-group coordination and make sure follow-up items from this report are tracked to completion.

**Questions and Feedback**

If you have questions about anything in this report, please raise them with your manager or through the usual internal channels. We value your input, particularly on how shared spaces and platforms are serving your work. The next report will follow the same format and will note any changes in progress, risks, or planned actions. Thank you to everyone whose steady work keeps these services and spaces running well for Zastama Industries.

Company-Wide Operations Status Report: Equipment, Services, and Platform Updates

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a periodic view of where several active efforts stand at Zastama Industries. Overall, work is moving steadily. Equipment delivery to our coastal site is progressing, a key services relationship is active, and our internal teams continue to coordinate well across locations. A few risks need attention, and they are covered below along with the next steps we plan to take.

The main themes this period are logistics for incoming equipment, the services work tied to one of our larger vendor relationships, leadership of a cross-functional initiative, and a welcome look at the people and teams who keep these efforts running.

**Progress**

*Equipment delivery.* Kremarel Partners delivers equipment to the Kimmoine Annex. Kremarel Partners has a contract worth $2.8M, which makes it one of the more significant commitments we are managing right now. The Kimmoine Annex is located in the coastal region, and that location shapes how we plan receiving, storage, and installation. Facilities and operations staff have been coordinating on receiving procedures so that incoming equipment can be checked, logged, and staged without disrupting other activity at the site. Coastal conditions also call for attention to handling and protection, so teams are reviewing how equipment is stored between arrival and commissioning.

*Services work.* Project Bilfael has a services contract with Kremarel Partners. This means the relationship with Kremarel Partners covers both physical equipment and ongoing services support. The project team has been working to keep the two streams aligned, so that service activities are sequenced sensibly against equipment arrivals. Regular check-ins between the project team, procurement, and finance help us track deliverables against contract terms and surface questions early.

*Initiative leadership.* Megea Fosaine leads Project Vebamett. She has been focused on establishing clear ownership across contributing groups, keeping stakeholders informed, and maintaining a shared view of priorities. Contributors from several functions are participating, and the emphasis this period has been on communication habits that reduce handoff delays. Colleagues who have questions about how Project Vebamett connects to their own work are encouraged to reach out to Megea Fosaine directly.

*Teams and people.* The Fonathe Platform Group works out of the Brerponen Annex. The group continues to support the shared technical foundations that other teams rely on, and its proximity to one another at the Brerponen Annex has helped with quick problem solving. We also want to recognize that Gonnom Gosmunza joined the company in 2023. Since then, Gonnom Gosmunza has become part of the fabric of our work, and we are glad to highlight that continued contribution as part of this report's focus on our people.

*Cross-cutting improvements.* Beyond the individual efforts above, several process improvements are underway. We are standardizing how status information is captured so that updates read consistently from one team to the next. We are also tightening our approach to documenting decisions, so that the reasoning behind choices is easy to find later. These are modest changes, but they reduce confusion and save time for everyone.

**Risks**

1. *Delivery coordination.* Because Kremarel Partners delivers equipment to the Kimmoine Annex, any change in delivery timing can ripple into installation and service scheduling. We are mitigating this by keeping communication open with the vendor and by maintaining flexibility in receiving plans.

2. *Coastal environment.* The coastal setting of the Kimmoine Annex introduces conditions that can affect equipment storage and handling. Teams should follow established protective practices and report any concerns promptly.

3. *Contract alignment.* With both equipment and services tied to Kremarel Partners, there is a risk that scope or schedule expectations drift between the two. Project Bilfael is responsible for watching this closely, and finance and procurement are supporting by reviewing the $2.8M contract against actual progress.

4. *Cross-team dependencies.* Project Vebamett relies on contributions from multiple groups, and the Fonathe Platform Group provides technical foundations that others depend on. If priorities collide, work can queue up. Leaders are reviewing capacity and agreeing on sequencing to avoid bottlenecks.

5. *Information flow.* As more efforts run in parallel across different sites, there is a risk that updates reach some people later than others. This report is one step toward addressing that, and we welcome suggestions for improving how information is shared.

**Next Steps**

- Operations and facilities will finalize receiving and staging plans for the Kimmoine Annex, including protective measures suited to the coastal region.
- Project Bilfael will continue regular reviews of its services contract with Kremarel Partners and will flag any scope or schedule concerns to leadership early.
- Megea Fosaine will continue to guide Project Vebamett, with a focus on clarifying responsibilities and keeping contributors aligned.
- The Fonathe Platform Group will keep supporting dependent teams from the Brerponen Annex and will share guidance on how to request support.
- Finance and procurement will keep tracking the $2.8M contract with Kremarel Partners against deliverables and report any variance.
- Managers will encourage their teams to adopt the shared status format so that future reports are even easier to read.

**Closing Note**

Thank you to everyone contributing to these efforts. If you have questions, observations, or ideas about anything in this report, please bring them to your manager or to the relevant project lead. The next periodic report will follow the same structure so that progress and risks can be compared over time.

Zastama Industries Periodic Status Report: Projects, Vendors, and Facilities Update

**Summary**

This report gives all employees a shared view of where several important efforts stand. It covers two projects, one analytics group, and two external relationships that support our operations. Overall, the picture is mixed. Some work is moving along steadily and some needs attention. We want everyone to understand the current state, the reasons behind it, and what happens next, so that questions can be raised early and handled in the open.

The headline items are these. Project Nuzeor is currently paused pending review, though it is still targeting completion in Q3 FY26. Project Vebamett is currently at risk. Kremarel Partners continues to deliver equipment to the Kimmoine Annex. Satisen Labs is up for renewal in Q2 FY27. Details on each follow below.

**Progress**

*Project Nuzeor.* Leroror Lukaine, a Research Lead, leads Project Nuzeor. The project is currently paused pending review. The pause is a deliberate checkpoint, not a cancellation. During the review, the team is looking at scope, assumptions, and dependencies so that work can restart on firm footing. The stated target remains completion in Q3 FY26. Because the project is paused, that target will depend on how quickly the review concludes and what it recommends. Leroror Lukaine will share the outcome of the review with the wider company once a decision has been made, and anyone with input relevant to the review should send it to her through their normal management channel.

*Dankenor Analytics Unit.* Pivoine Geltoett is a member of the Dankenor Analytics Unit. The unit continues to serve as a source of analysis and reporting for teams across the company. Colleagues who need analytical support should route requests through their managers so that the unit can prioritize them sensibly. We appreciate the steady contribution Pivoine Geltoett and the rest of the unit make to decision-making across the business.

*Equipment deliveries.* Kremarel Partners delivers equipment to the Kimmoine Annex. Deliveries are a routine but important part of keeping the site supplied, and the arrangement is working as intended. Staff who depend on incoming equipment should coordinate with the facilities lead on receiving and handling, so that arrivals are logged, inspected, and put to use without delay.

*Vendor agreement.* Satisen Labs holds a 36-month master services agreement with the company. That agreement provides a stable framework for the services we receive. The relationship is up for renewal in Q2 FY27. Renewal is still some time away, but early preparation will help us negotiate from an informed position. The procurement and finance leads will begin gathering usage information and feedback from the teams that rely on the services.

**Risks**

*Project Vebamett is currently at risk.* This is the most pressing concern in this report. We are treating the status seriously and want to be transparent about it. The at-risk designation means that outcomes the project owners expected are not assured under present conditions. The responsible leads are reviewing causes, weighing options, and deciding what support is needed. We will report further as the picture clarifies. Employees working on or alongside Project Vebamett should raise blockers promptly rather than waiting for a formal checkpoint.

*Project Nuzeor timing.* Because Project Nuzeor is paused pending review while still targeting completion in Q3 FY26, there is a schedule risk. If the review takes longer than hoped, or if it calls for changes in scope, the target may come under pressure. We will flag any change to the target as soon as it is known.

*Delivery and vendor dependencies.* Our reliance on Kremarel Partners for equipment arriving at the Kimmoine Annex means that any disruption in deliveries could affect downstream work. Likewise, with the renewal of Satisen Labs approaching in Q2 FY27, we need to avoid a last-minute scramble. Neither is a concern today, but both are worth watching.

**Next Steps**

1. Complete the review of Project Nuzeor and communicate the result, including whether the Q3 FY26 completion target holds, to all employees.
2. Continue assessing Project Vebamett, agree on corrective actions, and share an update on its status once those actions are set.
3. Keep supporting requests to the Dankenor Analytics Unit, with managers helping to prioritize what is sent to Pivoine Geltoett and her colleagues.
4. Maintain the delivery routine between Kremarel Partners and the Kimmoine Annex, and ask the facilities lead to report any delays or quality problems.
5. Start renewal preparation for Satisen Labs ahead of Q2 FY27, including collecting feedback on service quality, reviewing how the 36-month master services agreement has performed, and identifying terms worth revisiting.
6. Issue the next periodic report with updated status on each of the items above.

**How to Raise Questions**

If you have questions or information that bears on any item here, please speak with your manager or the relevant functional lead. Early, candid communication is the best way to keep risks small and progress steady. Thank you to everyone at Zastama Industries for the work that makes these efforts possible.

Zastama Industries Cross-Functional Program Update: Meeting Notes

**Date:** October 9, 2026
**Attendees:** Vadesis Gummenbel (Chief of Staff, facilitator), Krilfia Mukela (Solutions Architect), Megea Fosaine, a finance representative, a procurement representative, a representative of the Fonathe Platform Group, and a program management representative
**Distribution:** All employees

## Purpose

This meeting gave a short, shared view of where several cross-functional efforts stand, who is responsible for what, and which follow-ups are needed. Notes are circulated company-wide so that every team can see the same information and know where to direct questions.

## Discussion Points

**Opening and context**

Vadesis Gummenbel, who works as a Chief of Staff, opened the meeting by explaining why these notes go to the whole company. Several recent questions from employees showed that people were unsure who owns which area and how the larger efforts connect. The goal was to answer those questions in one place and to keep the tone practical.

**Project Stebril**

The group reviewed Project Stebril first. It has an approved budget of $7.2M, and it has a services contract with Misginine Systems. The finance representative confirmed that the budget figure is the number all teams should use when they discuss the project. The procurement representative noted that the services contract is in place, so the conversation shifted from vendor selection to vendor coordination.

Attendees discussed how to keep spending visible against the approved budget. The finance representative suggested a regular, lightweight reporting rhythm so that no team is surprised by cost movement. Krilfia Mukela, a Solutions Architect, said the technical design work should be documented clearly so that the services delivered under the contract can be checked against what was planned. She stressed that clear interface descriptions reduce rework, and rework is the most common source of avoidable cost on engagements like this.

The procurement representative added that anyone who needs to engage Misginine Systems should route requests through the project owner, rather than contacting the vendor directly. This avoids duplicate requests and keeps the contract scope clean.

**Project Nuzeor**

Next, the group discussed Project Nuzeor, which is targeting completion in Q3 FY26. The program management representative said the target remains the planning anchor and that dependencies should be raised early if any of them threaten it. No change to the target was proposed in this meeting. Attendees agreed that the main risk to any completion target is late discovery of dependencies, so teams were encouraged to flag blockers as soon as they appear instead of waiting for a scheduled review.

**Fleet telemetry ownership**

The representative of the Fonathe Platform Group reminded everyone that the Fonathe Platform Group is responsible for fleet telemetry. Questions about telemetry data, collection, or availability should go to that group first. This was raised because several teams had been unsure where to send telemetry requests, and some had tried to build their own workarounds. Attendees agreed that a single point of ownership will prevent duplicated effort and inconsistent data.

Krilfia Mukela noted that telemetry is also an important input to the architecture work on the larger efforts discussed today, so early alignment with the Fonathe Platform Group will help her team avoid late design changes.

**Incident response tooling**

Megea Fosaine, who joined the company in 2018, focuses on incident response tooling. She gave a brief overview of how her work relates to the other topics. Reliable telemetry makes incident response faster, and well-documented designs make it easier to find the cause of a problem when something breaks. She encouraged teams to tell her when their processes depend on tooling that may need to be adapted for incident handling. Several attendees said they appreciated hearing about her longer history with the company, because it helps them know whom to ask about how past issues were handled.

**Communication and coordination**

The group closed the discussion with a conversation about communication habits. Vadesis Gummenbel asked that status updates be written in plain language and avoid internal shorthand, since these notes and related updates reach employees in every function. Attendees agreed that a short written update is better than a long meeting when information is simple, and that meetings should be reserved for decisions and unresolved questions.

## Decisions

- The approved budget for Project Stebril, $7.2M, will be treated as the single reference figure in all company communications about the project.
- Requests involving Misginine Systems will be routed through the project owner and not made directly by individual teams.
- Project Nuzeor will continue to plan against its current target of Q3 FY26, and teams will raise dependency risks as soon as they are identified.
- Fleet telemetry questions will be directed to the Fonathe Platform Group as the owning group.
- Megea Fosaine will serve as the first point of contact for questions about incident response tooling.
- Status communications going to the whole company will use plain language.

## Action Items

- **Finance representative:** Set up a simple recurring view of spending against the approved budget for Project Stebril and share it with the project owner.
- **Procurement representative:** Send a short note to relevant teams explaining how to route requests involving Misginine Systems.
- **Krilfia Mukela:** Make sure the technical design documentation for Project Stebril is current and shareable, and review telemetry-related design assumptions with the Fonathe Platform Group.
- **Representative of the Fonathe Platform Group:** Publish a brief guide describing how teams can submit fleet telemetry requests.
- **Program management representative:** Collect dependency risks for Project Nuzeor and report any threat to the Q3 FY26 target at the next review.
- **Megea Fosaine:** Gather input from teams on tooling needs related to incident response and summarize the themes.
- **Vadesis Gummenbel:** Circulate these notes to all employees and schedule the next cross-functional update.

2. Say what good looks like. Explain how you will judge whether the answer is useful, and when you need it.

Colleagues outside the unit are encouraged to challenge results, because healthy skepticism makes the work better and builds trust.

Overall, the effort is moving steadily. The core design questions have been narrowed, and the remaining work is mostly about validation, documentation, and agreeing on rollout sequencing with the teams that will depend on the tooling. **Ownership and funding.** Spending for the work is tracked under a single budget line. The budget code for Pethisa Hebroren is SP-9062-V, and all related costs continue to be reported against it. The finance lead has not raised any reconciliation issues this period.

**Tooling work.** The group has continued refining how retention rules are defined, applied, and audited. Work this period centered on making policy definitions easier to review, tightening the way deletion and archival actions are logged, and clarifying which datasets fall under which rules. Early internal testing has surfaced several edge cases around datasets with mixed retention requirements, and these are being triaged.

**Analytical support.** Thikama Harlurine, a Data Scientist who joined the company in 2023, has been supporting the effort by examining how data is actually used and aged across the datasets in scope. Her analysis is informing which retention categories are practical and where the current definitions are too coarse. **Coordination.** Discussions with legal and compliance contacts have continued. The main outcome is a shared understanding of the review process for any retention rule that changes how long sensitive records are kept. A security reviewer has also asked to see the audit logging approach before it is finalized.

## Risks

1. **Ambiguous requirements.** Some retention obligations are interpreted differently by different stakeholders. If these are not resolved soon, rules may need to be reworked after testing, which would cost time.
2. **Dataset complexity.** Datasets with mixed requirements may need to be split or tagged more granularly. This could expand scope if the number of affected datasets is larger than expected.
3. **Dependency timing.** Downstream teams have their own priorities, and their availability for integration testing is uncertain. Delays there could push back the rollout sequence.
4. **Irreversible actions.** Deletion is inherently hard to undo. Until safeguards and review steps are fully validated, we are keeping the tooling in a conservative, non-destructive mode for anything beyond test data.
5. **Capacity.** Analytical and engineering effort is concentrated among a few people. Absence or competing requests could slow progress.

## Next Steps

- Resolve the open interpretation questions with legal and compliance, and record the decisions in writing.
- Incorporate the latest usage analysis from Thikama Harlurine into a revised set of retention categories.
- Complete the review of audit logging with the security reviewer and address any feedback.

- Agree on a rollout sequence with downstream teams, including a clear checkpoint before any destructive action is enabled outside of test data.
- Prepare a short follow-up for the next reporting period, covering decisions made, remaining risks, and any change in resourcing needs.

This session was kept small on purpose. It covered work that touches both payments reconciliation and demand forecasting, and the attendees agreed the details are not yet ready for wider circulation within Zastama Industries.

## Background

Zosne Bramfa focuses on payments reconciliation, and her work is charged to cost center JD-4128-T. Pethisa Hebroren reports to Zosne Bramfa and handles much of the day-to-day matching work that supports that focus. Liluan Nemlurel joined the company in 2016 and focuses on demand forecasting models. The finance representative attended to confirm how any shared work would be accounted for and to flag controls that finance would expect to see.

## Discussion Points

1. **Overlap between reconciliation and forecasting.** Liluan Nemlurel explained that the forecasting models are sensitive to the timing of recorded payments. When payments are matched late or booked against the wrong period, the inputs to the models drift. Zosne Bramfa agreed that the reconciliation process can be a source of that drift and said the group should understand where the delays occur before proposing fixes.

2. **Current reconciliation workflow.** Pethisa Hebroren walked through how unmatched items are currently identified and worked. Items that cannot be matched automatically are reviewed by hand, and the backlog tends to grow near period end. Pethisa Hebroren noted that the exception categories are not applied consistently, which makes it hard to report on the causes of delay.

3. **What forecasting actually needs.** Liluan Nemlurel clarified that the models do not require perfect reconciliation. They need a dependable signal about which recent payments are still unresolved, so the models can treat those figures with appropriate caution. Zosne Bramfa said that a simple status flag on unresolved items might meet this need without changing the wider process.

4. **Finance expectations.** The finance representative stressed that any new flag or shared data feed must not alter the ledger or bypass existing approvals. Costs of any shared effort should be tracked transparently. Zosne Bramfa confirmed that work done by her group on this topic would continue to be recorded against the same cost center unless finance advised otherwise.

5. **Data sharing and access.** The group briefly discussed who should see reconciliation exception data. The consensus was that access should be limited to the people doing the work for now, with a broader review later once the approach is validated.

6. **Risks.** Attendees identified two risks: inconsistent exception labeling could undermine the flag, and an extra manual step could add to the period-end backlog. Neither was considered a blocker, but both need an owner.

## Decisions

- The group will pursue a lightweight "unresolved" status signal rather than a redesign of the reconciliation process.
- Exception categories will be standardized before the signal is built, so the data is reliable.
- Access to the exception data stays restricted to the working group during the initial phase.
- No changes will be made to ledger entries or approval steps as part of this effort.

## Risks

1. **Audit closure timing.** The remediation tied to the audit finding depends on reviewers being available to examine evidence. If review slots slip, closure could drift even though the technical work is complete. Mitigation: request reviewer availability early and keep the evidence package current.

2. **Reconciliation complexity.** Payments reconciliation has many edge cases, and some depend on decisions that sit outside the group, such as policy on how long unresolved exceptions may remain open. Without those decisions, engineers may build to assumptions that later need rework. Mitigation: ask the finance lead for a policy answer and record it in the design notes.

3. **Capacity concentration.** Specialized knowledge about reconciliation is concentrated in a small number of people. If one of them becomes unavailable, progress on that area could slow. Mitigation: encourage documentation and pairing so that knowledge spreads across the group.

4. **External dependency.** The vendor-facing integration discussion remains unresolved. Delays there could affect integration testing. Mitigation: set a clear decision point with the vendor and prepare a fallback approach for testing.

5. **Scope pressure.** Requests from adjacent teams continue to arrive. Taking on too many could dilute focus. Mitigation: route new requests through the existing planning session and weigh them against current commitments.
